name: Design by Contract and Defensive Programming
intent: Decide, for every function, who is responsible for what: what callers must supply, what the function promises, and what always stays true. Check untrusted input at the boundary, and use internal checks to find bugs rather than to hide them.
scenario: An order passes through four layers: an API, a service, a pricing function and a ledger. Out of 20 requests, 4 carry nonsense from a user and 2 hit a bug in the service that multiplies a price by 100. One team checks nothing. Another checks every value in every layer. A third clamps bad values into range and carries on. Two designs stop all six bad requests, one at several times the cost of the other, and a third reports no errors at all while 6 of the 20 requests are wrong.
problem: Defensive programming says: do not trust your inputs. Design by contract says: make the trust explicit. Both are right and both are easy to misapply. Checking every value in every function looks safe, but it repeats the same rule in several places, costs time on every call, and teaches nobody which layer owns the rule. Repairing bad values quietly looks robust, but it hides the bug and produces a wrong answer that looks right. The useful question is not 'should I check?' but 'who is responsible for this condition, and what should happen when it fails?'

howItWorks.title: Write the contract in three parts
howItWorks.text: A precondition is what the caller must make true before the call: quantity between 1 and 100. A postcondition is what the function promises on return: the total is between 0 and the order limit. An invariant is what stays true across calls: a ledger never holds a negative balance. A broken precondition is a bug in the caller, a broken postcondition is a bug in the function. That split is what makes a failure easy to place.

howItWorks.title: Draw the trust boundary
howItWorks.text: Data from outside, such as user input, files and other systems, cannot be trusted and must be validated, with a friendly error. Data produced by your own code is a different matter: if it is wrong, that is a bug, and the right response is to fail loudly where it is first visible. In the simulation, with 20% bad user input and 10% bugs in our own code, validating at the boundary costs 260 checks per 100 requests.

howItWorks.title: Check everywhere and pay for it
howItWorks.text: The over-applied extreme is to validate every parameter in every layer. It catches the same 100% of bad requests, but costs 940 checks per 100 requests, 12 for every good one, mostly repeating verdicts already reached. It also puts the rule about quantity in 4 places, so changing the limit means 4 edits and a risk that one is missed and the layers disagree.

howItWorks.title: Never repair silently
howItWorks.text: Clamping a quantity of -3 to 1, or an impossible total to the limit, makes errors disappear from the logs and appear in the books. The program keeps running, and it keeps running wrongly: in the run, the repair design reports no failures and 6 of 20 requests are wrong. Repair is only right when the repaired value is the correct answer by specification, such as a UI slider that stops at its maximum. Otherwise reject, or fail.

howItWorks.title: Know what an assertion is for
howItWorks.text: Internal contract checks are usually assertions: they find bugs during development and testing, and many languages and build modes disable them in production, for example Python with -O or C and C++ with NDEBUG. That is fine for conditions that can only fail through a bug, and wrong for validating anything that comes from outside. With internal checks off, the contract design still catches user mistakes at the boundary, but the 10 bugs per 100 requests become wrong records instead of loud failures.

pros: A failure points at the layer and the party at fault: caller or function
Each rule has one owner, so changing a limit is one edit
Checks at the boundary give users clear errors, and checks inside find bugs early
Contracts double as documentation and as test oracles
cons: Writing and maintaining contracts takes discipline, and a wrong contract gives false confidence
Few mainstream languages enforce contracts, so they live in assertions, types and conventions
Failing loudly inside a service means a bug becomes an error response, which needs handling
Boundary validation must be complete: a missed path lets bad input reach code that trusted it
whenToUse: Any function with conditions on its inputs or results that callers could otherwise misunderstand
A clear boundary where outside data enters: validate once there, in one place
Core invariants such as money, inventory or permissions, where silent wrong answers are expensive
whenNotToUse: Repeating checks in every layer by habit, for values a lower layer cannot receive in a bad state
Using assertions to validate user input or anything that must still be checked in production
Repairing invalid input by default, unless the repair is the specified behaviour
pitfalls: Checking everywhere and trusting nowhere: the rule is copied into several layers, the layers drift apart, and nobody knows which one is authoritative
Silent repair, such as clamping or substituting a default: the bug stops being visible and starts being wrong data
Using assertions for input validation, then running in a mode where assertions are removed and the validation vanishes with them
Validating at the boundary but not at every boundary: a batch import, an admin tool or a message consumer that skips the check
Putting side effects inside a check, so that turning checks off changes what the program does
Returning a polite error for a bug in your own code and carrying on: a postcondition failure should be loud, logged and investigated
Strengthening a precondition in a subclass, so a caller that was valid for the base type is now rejected: the contract view of the Liskov principle

roles.label: Caller
roles.description: The user or code that makes the request and owes the preconditions.

roles.label: Boundary
roles.description: The layer where untrusted data enters and is validated once.

roles.label: Inner layers
roles.description: Service and pricing code, which promise postconditions and trust their callers.

roles.label: Ledger
roles.description: The record that must never hold a wrong value.

quiz.question: A pricing function's postcondition says the total is between 0 and the order limit. It returns 300,000 for a limit of 100,000. Whose bug is this, in contract terms?
options: The caller's, because it should have checked the total before calling.
The user's, because they entered a quantity that was too high.
The pricing function's, because it broke its own promise.
Nobody's, because contracts only describe what callers must supply.
quiz.explanation: A broken precondition points at the caller, a broken postcondition at the function. Here the caller supplied valid input and the function returned a result it promised never to return.

quiz.question: Why is 'validate every parameter in every layer' a poor default for internal calls?
options: Checks are never fast enough for production code.
It repeats the same rule in several places, costs checks on every call, and hides which layer owns the rule.
Internal code cannot receive bad values, so a check is always a bug.
It makes the code stop on the first bad input, when it should carry on.
quiz.explanation: Repeated checks drift apart and cost time, and when one layer's rule changes, the others must follow. Validate untrusted input once at the boundary, and use a few well-placed internal checks to find bugs.

quiz.question: A service clamps a negative quantity to 1 and continues, so no request ever fails. What is the likely result?
options: More robust behaviour, because the program never crashes.
A faster program, because it skips the error path.
The same results as rejecting, since a quantity of 1 is the nearest valid value.
Errors vanish from the logs but appear in the data, as orders for the wrong quantity.
quiz.explanation: Silent repair keeps the program running and makes the wrong answer look right. Unless clamping is the specified behaviour, reject the input or fail, so the mistake is seen where it happens.
